blocks.text: Cobalt Instrument Studio demonstrates how a single, coherent telemetry model can support an industrial display, reproducible fault scenarios, and inspectable diagnostic behavior. The implementation runs entirely in the visitor's browser as a static React and TypeScript application. It provides a working exploration environment for instrumentation and software design.

The local implementation includes six synchronized instruments, four operating modes, three replayable scenarios, validated thresholds, acknowledgment and recovery rules, bounded history, local settings, and CSV export. Validation recorded {{unitPassed}} unit tests and {{browserPassed}} browser tests passing. Public hosting, hardware integration, and production validation remain outside the implemented capability.

blocks.text: Simulation scope

SIMULATED - NOT LIVE EQUIPMENT. Every instrument value is generated locally. The interface is a display and simulator, with no backend, device connection, equipment command path, user authentication, or safety control. The telemetry relationships are engineering assumptions for this demonstration; they are not calibrated equipment measurements.

One typed reducer owns the session. Modes and guided scenarios supply commands to a seeded engine model. Simulated transport determines whether a new sample is delivered. Gauges, diagnostic rules, the chart, and export consume the same last received telemetry, so a communication interruption freezes displayed values without stopping the internal model.

blocks.text: The engine and diagnostic rules are pure modules under src/engine. Components render reducer state. LocalStorage stores only validated settings. Charts and events stay in bounded memory, and exports download through browser Blob URLs. No server API or network data source is required during site operation.

The model advances by a fixed 0.5 simulated seconds per delivered timer step. This preserves exact seeded replay even if wall-clock scheduling varies. Pause stops simulation time and timeout age. The 500 ms interval is a configured target, not a real-time scheduling guarantee; background tabs may be throttled.

blocks.text: Time and units

Canonical model units are rpm, psi, degrees F, V, and percent. Metric display converts pressure to kPa and temperature to degrees C without changing model values or diagnostic thresholds. The settings editor explicitly retains canonical threshold units. Scenario fault kinetics are accelerated for inspection and do not establish a physical time constant.
Bounded retention

Sample history retains at most 240 received samples, representing up to roughly 120 simulated seconds at full delivery. The timestamp span can be longer across an outage because missing samples are not appended. Events retain at most 100 records. The trend leaves a gap across undelivered samples rather than interpolating a false trace.
Model limitations

There is no engine shutdown model, sensor calibration, noise characterization from hardware, environmental model, fuel mass balance, or validated charging circuit. Seeded disturbance provides repeatability, not statistical realism. Fault values and display ranges support an explanatory demonstration and must not be reused as equipment operating limits.
Normal operating ramp

Expected behavior: begin at idle, raise speed and load smoothly, let oil pressure follow, and retain slow thermal response. Observed with seed 27041 at 35 simulated seconds: RPM {{normalRPM}}, load {{normalLoad}} percent, oil {{normalOil}} psi, and coolant {{normalCoolant}} degrees F. No threshold transition occurred under the default rules. Replay resets the model, history, and diagnostics to the same sequence while retaining preferences.
Coolant overheat

Expected behavior: cooling degradation begins at 6 s and progressively crosses warning and critical thresholds. Observed transitions were normal to warning at 14.0 s with 223.5 degrees F, then warning to critical at 18.5 s with 236.8 degrees F. The default boundaries are 220 and 235 degrees F with a 4 degree F recovery margin and two received samples of debounce. At 35 s the model reached {{overheatCoolant}} degrees F. Browser checks acknowledged the warning, verified renewed acknowledgment after escalation, and reset the session to normal.
Communication loss

Expected behavior: drop delivered samples from 5 s through 16.5 s while the central model continues. The final sample before the gap was received at 4.5 s. Observed timeout onset was 6.5 s, exactly 2 simulated seconds after that sample. Gauges retained stale received values and history stopped growing. At 17 s a fresh sample arrived and the communication condition resolved automatically. The recovered trend preserved the delivery gap.
Rule state and acknowledgment

Each channel maintains one normal, warning, or critical state. Hysteresis defines a separate recovery boundary; configurable debounce requires consecutive received samples. Stale duplicates do not count toward telemetry debounce. Communication timeout is immediate when its age boundary is reached. Transition events explain the triggering value and threshold. Acknowledgment records review, leaves the continuing condition active, and resets on escalation or recovery. Sustained alerts are deduplicated to prevent event floods.

All timestamps above are simulation time. Automated guided browser checks used a controlled clock. These observations establish application behavior for a defined seed and settings, not real machinery response or field communications reliability.

Local validation completed {{unitPassed}} unit checks and {{browserPassed}} browser checks with zero failures in the final baseline. TypeScript and production compilation were checked separately. Tests exercise behavior through both the pure engine and the actual rendered application.

Production JavaScript totaled {{jsBytes}} bytes ({{jsGzipBytes}} bytes gzip); CSS totaled {{cssBytes}} bytes. In one desktop smoke check, the simulation clock reached 3 s after {{wallMs}} ms of wall time including interaction overhead, with no page errors. This measures one workflow, not interval accuracy.

Browser tests took {{browserDuration}} s; unit test bodies took {{unitDuration}} s. Heap, frame rate, browser soak, hardware timing, and public availability were not measured. Buffer caps do not prove a total heap bound.

The project makes instrumentation behavior reviewable without access to equipment. A real industrial deployment would require separate integration, safety, security, and reliability engineering. The comparison below identifies future work rather than claiming production readiness.

blocks.text: Design tradeoffs

A static frontend keeps operation inspectable and avoids server, credential, and device dependencies. One central reducer makes relationships and replay behavior explicit. Fixed steps favor deterministic demonstration over real-time fidelity. Bounded buffers keep retention deliberate, while memory-only telemetry avoids implying durable records. A single selectable chart and three simple views keep the scope focused.

The application can help evaluate a display or diagnostic workflow before implementing equipment connectivity. It cannot command a physical machine, prove a hardware fault, certify an alarm policy, or replace an operational monitoring system.

pages.title: Generic applications and future engineering work

blocks.text: Operator workflow examples

Generator instrumentation training: an operator can run the normal ramp, compare speed, pressure, and load, then follow an overheat escalation without connecting equipment. Production use would require validated sensor mapping, equipment-specific thresholds, and a separate control/safety design.

Fleet diagnostic review: a reviewer can inspect stale readings, acknowledge a communication alert, and trace recovery events. A real fleet system would need authenticated multi-device identity, reliable timestamps, durable records, and permissions.

Pump or motor condition-display prototyping: a designer can evaluate layout, readable units, fault presentation, and replay behavior. Real application would require a different validated telemetry model, physical sensors, hardware tests, and failure analysis.
Prioritized potential improvements

P0: real gateway/fieldbus adapter; validated telemetry schema; hardware in the loop; connectivity security hardening; expanded end to end and cross-browser tests. These establish prerequisites for receiving real data safely and interpreting it correctly.

P1: advanced fault injection; historical storage; alert routing; role based access; audit trails; multi-device support; device configuration. Each is future work beyond the implemented browser session and three basic replays.

P2: performance profiling; formal accessibility audit; automated release safeguards. The separate roadmap gives engineering benefit and rough Small/Medium/Large complexity for all 15 proposed improvements. No delivery commitment is implied.
Version and publication state

Version 0.1.0 is prepared locally. CI, GitHub Pages deployment, issue forms, and a tag-triggered release workflow are present but have not run remotely. Netlify production is the intended primary shareable endpoint and Pages is the independent backup. Public repository creation, commits/pushes, site deployment, and the v0.1.0 tag/release require a separate authorized publication step after inspection.

Both hosted builds will serve static assets and downloadable reports, without requiring the development computer to remain powered on. Provider permissions, quotas, plan limits, and future availability must be checked during publication; no uptime guarantee or verified public endpoint exists yet.
